Hami melons are sweet, crisp melons from the oases of Xinjiang, named after Hami, the oasis at the eastern gate of Xinjiang on the road into China. Chinese tradition says melons from the Western Regions reached the Han court as tribute in the reign of Emperor Ming (58 to 75), when Han armies were pushing back into the region against the Xiongnu. The details of that early tribute are hard to confirm.

Tribute of this kind was both a gift and a sign of loyalty: oasis rulers sent rare local goods and received silk and titles in return. The name Hami melon is much later. The story goes that in the late 1600s the ruler of Hami sent melons to the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing, who named them after the place.

Hot dry summers, cold nights and snowmelt water make the oases ideal melon country, and Hami melons are still a symbol of Xinjiang.
